question: Which concrete algorithms do one-block Transformers learn for per-token histogram counting, and how do attention type, softmax, BOS tokens, embedding dimension, and feed-forward width determine the feasible solution?

key_findings.claim: The paper identifies two qualitatively different exact counting mechanisms whose resource demands fall on different components.
key_findings.evidence: Relation-based counting uses dot-product comparisons to encode how many tokens equal the query token and needs only one hidden feed-forward unit in the orthogonal-embedding regime. Inventory-based counting uses mixing for aggregation and a feed-forward lookup table spanning the alphabet, requiring hidden width at least T. Explicit parameter constructions accompany the mechanistic interpretations.

key_findings.claim: Minor architectural choices change which algorithm is available: BOS-enabled or unnormalized dot-product attention supports relation-based counting, whereas row-wise softmax can force a dot-product model toward the wider inventory solution.
key_findings.evidence: For d at least T, Proposition 4.1 constructs perfect BOS and BOS-plus-softmax models with p=1; Proposition 4.2 obtains a p=1 solution without BOS using a tagged counting direction. In contrast, softmax normalization removes a sequence-common counting direction for dot-plus-softmax, and learned near-perfect models appear when p and d scale with T, consistent with alphabet inventory stored in the feed-forward layer.

anchors.section: Dot-product attention with softmax and inventory-based counting

key_findings.claim: Orthogonal token embeddings are sufficient but not necessary because discrete output margins and softmax concentration can tolerate or suppress interference in compressed embeddings.
key_findings.evidence: The mutual-coherence analysis propagates non-orthogonality error to a decision-margin condition. Proposition 4.5 constructs BOS-plus-softmax or dot-plus-softmax solutions with d at least ceil(log2(T+1))+2; for T=32 and L=10 this predicts d=7 near the most efficient learned solutions. A d=4 construction exists but requires increasingly extreme softmax temperature and was hand-built rather than learned.

key_findings.claim: Large hyperparameter sweeps and weight introspection reproduce the predicted phase structure, but evidence is confined to a synthetic, noncausal, shallow counting task.
key_findings.evidence: For T=32, L=10, five runs across grids of d and p show sharp architecture-dependent transitions and learned attention/MLP geometry resembling the constructions. Ablations over T in {15,32,64}, L in {5,10,15,30}, and two-layer blocks largely preserve the pattern, although fixed training budget weakens performance at L=30. The authors explicitly exclude causal masks, positional encodings, autoregressive generation, and realistic depth.

method.core_idea: Triangulate a toy Transformer's learned algorithm using exact constructive solutions, architecture/width phase diagrams, and mechanistic inspection of attention, embeddings, and feed-forward responses.
method.mechanism: One-layer residual models with linear or dot-product token mixing, optional softmax/BOS, learned d-dimensional embeddings, and a p-wide ReLU MLP are trained online on histogram sequences. Analytic constructions assign component roles for relation- and inventory-based counting; mutual-coherence bounds characterize compressed embeddings. Sweeps over d, p, T, L, and a two-layer extension test whether learned solutions occupy the predicted regimes.
assumptions: Sequences are permutation-equivariant i.i.d. samples from a fixed finite alphabet and require no positions or causal masking.
Exact constructions initially assume infinite numerical precision and, in several regimes, mutually orthogonal token embeddings.
A categorical count can remain correct whenever interference leaves logits inside the discrete class margin.
Attention/value simplifications and a single hidden-layer MLP preserve the component interaction of interest.
Similarity between inspected learned geometry and a construction is evidence for, but not a causal proof of, the implemented algorithm.

techniques.role: Provides exact weights for multiple attention/MLP architectures that solve histogram counting.
Maps accuracy over embedding dimension and feed-forward width for each token mixer.
Tests attention scores and feed-forward responses on controlled mixtures of learned embeddings.
Relates token-embedding interference and output margins to sufficient compressed dimension.
Suppresses unequal-token interference enough to count with binary-like embeddings.

evaluations.setting: Histogram task with T=32 tokens and L=10 over a dense grid of d and p
evaluations.metric: Per-position count accuracy over 3,000 fresh samples, averaged over five runs
evaluations.result: Near-perfect regions and parameter-efficiency frontiers depend sharply on mixer, softmax, and BOS; learned transition boundaries broadly match the constructions.
evaluations.baseline: Linear mixing, dot-product mixing, and BOS variants with or without softmax

evaluations.setting: Mechanistic probes of trained near-perfect models
evaluations.metric: Attention structure, responses to synthetic embedding mixtures, embedding overlaps, and MLP singular values
evaluations.result: BOS/dot models expose a scalar count direction, while linear and dot-plus-softmax models show alphabet-indexed MLP behavior consistent with inventory storage.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's exact relation-based and inventory-based weight constructions

evaluations.metric: Accuracy phase diagrams across T={15,32,64} and L={5,10,15,30}
evaluations.result: The main regimes persist across most settings and two layers, with weaker convergence for L=30 under the unchanged budget.

limitations: The task is a fixed-alphabet synthetic histogram, so it does not establish the same component roles for sorting, lookup, arithmetic, or language.
Models are one- or two-layer nonautoregressive encoders without positional embeddings or causal masks.
Several constructions rely on infinite precision or temperatures that worsen with sequence/alphabet size and may be numerically unlearnable.
The empirical study tests finite T and L with a fixed 500-epoch budget; it does not establish length or vocabulary extrapolation.
Weight geometry matching a proposed mechanism is not backed by necessity/sufficiency interventions on every trained model, especially where mechanisms may be superposed.
Parameter counts and exact task accuracy do not capture optimization cost, finite-precision robustness, or real inference efficiency.
failure_modes: Non-orthogonal embeddings entangle different token counts and systematically overcount repeated items.
Softmax normalization destroys a shared linear count direction, forcing an under-width MLP to fail.
High-temperature softmax overflows, saturates, or becomes impossible to learn at larger L and T.
Training selects an inventory solution even when a leaner relation circuit exists, or forms an uninterpretable superposition of both.
A construction perfect at a fixed length loses its decision margin under longer sequences or lower numerical precision.
Causal masking or positional features prevent the global aggregation assumed by the noncausal circuit.
reusable_insights: Analyze attention and MLP jointly: capacity moved out of one component must often reappear in the other.
Use explicit constructive circuits to predict phase boundaries before interpreting trained weights.
Distinguish representational sufficiency from learnability and finite-precision robustness.
Probe competing mechanisms with synthetic activation mixtures, not attention visualizations alone.
Treat BOS tokens and normalization as computational resources that can change the available algorithm.
Map algorithmic tasks over both representation dimension and hidden memory capacity rather than total parameters only.
open_questions: Do causal, autoregressive Transformers learn analogous relation/inventory circuits for online counting?
Which intervention can distinguish a true superposition from one dominant mechanism plus incidental features?
Can training be biased toward the relation-based solution when both are representable?
How do quantization, floating-point format, and softmax stabilization change the theoretical phase boundaries?
Do the same attention/MLP capacity substitutions govern sorting, lookup, and compositional algorithms?
Can these small-model mechanisms be located causally in subspaces of large language models?

competitive_landscape.title: Thinking Like Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: RASP programs histogram and related sequence operations and bounds layers/heads needed for compilation. The reviewed work asks which of several low-level constructions gradient training actually approaches and how d, p, softmax, and BOS redistribute the computation.

competitive_landscape.title: When Can Transformers Count to n?
competitive_landscape.difference: Yehudai et al. study context-dependent token counting and derive a context-length-related capacity transition and finite-precision obstruction. The reviewed paper offers a finer component-level taxonomy over histogram counting, but its exact high-temperature constructions share the same numerical-scaling concern.

competitive_landscape.title: Contextual Counting: A Mechanistic Study of Transformers on a Quantitative Task
competitive_landscape.difference: Golkar et al. compare causal/noncausal attention, positional encodings, bias-token mechanisms, and out-of-distribution behavior on contextual counting. The reviewed paper instead isolates attention/MLP capacity exchange and embedding geometry on the simpler global histogram task.

novelty_assessment: The relation-versus-inventory taxonomy, exact cross-architecture constructions, and empirical phase diagrams make a strong mechanistic case that seemingly small design choices move an algorithm between attention and MLP memory. RASP and concurrent counting theory already establish transformer countability and finite-capacity limits, while contextual-counting work covers causal and positional effects. The distinctive contribution is therefore the component-capacity tradeoff and learned-mechanism triangulation, with generality beyond this toy task still open.
reviewer_notes: Read all 33 extracted pages, including main proofs at the proposition level, mechanistic figures, limitations, and T/L/two-layer appendices. Claims about learned algorithms are phrased as consistency with probes rather than definitive circuit identification. Three primary arXiv competitors were checked on 2026-08-23.
